Dear hmecology and spatialcapturerecapture lists,

We will run a two-day workshop on NIMBLE at UC Berkeley in early June, 2020.  Pre-registration is available.

-Perry

---------- Forwarded message ---------
From: Chris Paciorek <christophe...@gmail.com>
Date: Wed, Dec 11, 2019 at 11:08 AM
Subject: NIMBLE short course, June 3-4, 2020 at UC Berkeley
To: nimble-users <nimble...@googlegroups.com>, <nimble-...@googlegroups.com>

Hi nimble-users, nimble-announce,

We’ll be holding a two-day training workshop on NIMBLE <https://r-nimble.org>, June 3-4, 2020 in Berkeley, California.  Please spread the word to anyone you think might be interested.

The tutorial will cover
the basic concepts and workflows for using NIMBLE and converting BUGS or JAGS models to work in NIMBLE.
overview of different MCMC sampling strategies and how to use them in NIMBLE.
writing new distributions and functions for more flexible modeling and more efficient computation.
tips and tricks for improving computational efficiency.
using advanced model components, including Bayesian non-parametric distributions (based on Dirichlet process priors), conditional auto-regressive (CAR) models for spatially correlated random fields, and reversible jump samplers for variable selection.
an introduction to programming new algorithms in NIMBLE.
calling R and compiled C++ code from compiled NIMBLE models or functions.

If participant interests vary sufficiently, the second half-day will be split into two tracks. One of these will likely focus on ecological models. The other will be chosen based on attendee interest from topics such as (a) advanced NIMBLE programming including writing new MCMC samplers, (b) advanced spatial or Bayesian non-parametric modeling, or (c) non-MCMC algorithms in NIMBLE such as sequential Monte Carlo.  Prior to the workshop, we will survey attendee interests and adjust content to meet attendee interests.

If you are interested in attending, please pre-register to hold a spot at https://forms.gle/6AtNgfdUdvhni32Q6.  The form also asks if you are interested in a relatively cheap dormitory-style housing option.  No payment is necessary to pre-register. Fees to finalize registration will be $230 (regular) or $115 (student).  We hope to be able to offer student travel awards; more information will follow.

The workshop will assume attendees have a basic understanding of hierarchical/Bayesian models and MCMC, the BUGS (or JAGS) model language, and some familiarity with R.

messages.body_plain:
Hi All,

I am relatively new to occupancy modeling and I am currently working on some multi-species occupancy models. I have a question about including categorical explanatory variables for replicates samples/surveys. Apologies in advance if this question is answered somewhere, I have not been able to find an answer yet.

Is it statistically sound to include replicate surveys of a site which all have unique categorical explanatory variables? Each site was surveyed multiple times, but there are no replicates for each categorical variable within each site. See example below.

                                             Categorical Variable

Site 1 –     Survey 1               x1

                Survey 2               x2

                Survey 3               x3

Site 2 –     Survey 1               x1

                Survey 2               x2

                Survey 3               x3

Site 3 –     Survey 1               x1

                Survey 2               x2

   Survey 3               x3

Site 4 –    Survey 1               x1

                Survey 2               x2

   Survey 3               x3

…

If so, how does this affect the inferences you are able to make about the effect of this categorical variable, detection and occupancy?

Thank you very much,

Bea

Hi Bea,
Can you clarify a little, are you collecting separate categorical variables in each visit?  Or does the same categorical variable have a different value in each visit?  The former case could be treated as missing data and there are various ways of tackling that problem in estimation.  The latter case may lead to confounding, as Kery mentions.  If you have complete confounding there is no point in trying to estimate an effect for both of the confounded variables, in this case survey visit and variable x.  Just pick 1 and understand that any observed effect could be attributable to either factor.

Cheers,
Dominic

messages.subject_clean: Hierarchical Bayesian models with Laplace Approximation
messages.body_plain:
Hello all,

I work with very large datasets, and I am interested in seeing if I can use Laplace Approximation with some of the more complex hierarchical Bayesian models to try to speed things up a bit. I can find plenty of information on how to fit simple linear models, random effects models, and models with spatial correlation using the R-INLA package. However, the package relies on model formulas similar to those used in the lm() and glmr() commands in R, and I have been unable to find methods for fitting even basic occupancy models or binomial N-mixture models as they would be specified in BUGS language. So for this I have two questions:
Are there any packages that can handle such models with Laplace approximation?, and
Is this even a good thing to do?

I have not seen this discussed here before, so any information I can get would be very much appreciated.

Thank you in advance,

Andrew D. Crosby

Postdoctoral Fellow

Boreal Avian Modelling Project

University of Alberta

Edmonton, AB

Well, you can fit site covariates on p, but not observational covariates. In their example they show that averaging an observational covariate to become a site-covariate and using that in the model for p did not lead to much difference in the inferences from those from the "full" model, but I bet this will not always be so.

Unfortunately, this seems to be a fundamental limitation in the INLA method and hence, my take is that INLA is not generally a method for fitting Nmix models.

But perhaps the Laplace approximation could still be used in a custom method coded up in, say, Nimble or Stan or greta ?

Best regards  --- Marc

messages.subject_clean: occupancy model: does leaving out a latent variable (hierarchy level) result in an equivalent model?
messages.body_plain:
Hello all!

Perhaps a trivial question, but I need to go back to basics :-) Sorry
if I missed it on Marc's trainings :-)

Say we have an occupancy model formulated as hierarchical bayesian model:

z[i] ~ dbern(pi[i])
logit(pi[i]) = .... # linear function of covariates for site i

y[i,j] ~ dbern(z[i] * p[i,j])

Because the only input data are the y[i,j] and we actually don't know
z[i] , I thought we could simplify (flatten) the model by removing the
latent variable z[] and having just:

y[i,j] ~ dbern(pi[i] * p[i,j])

The question is: Is this model equivalent to the first one?
y-prediction-wise, coefficient-wise, everything-wise (of course
everything except having z[] :-) If no, where is the difference?

I posted the question here with more detail, feel free to respond
there if you like https://stats.stackexchange.com/q/441829/5509

My thoughts are:

 - maybe it should be equivalent, because z[] is latent, so it should
be "integrated out" :-)
 - maybe it shouldn't, because z[i] could actually transfer
information between y[i,j] of the same site i. For example, when
y[i,1] = 1, the model will immediatelly know z[i] = 1 without
question, so this could somehow influence the inference for nodes
y[i,2], y[i,3] etc... But maybe this will not influence the overall
result at all (?)

Thanks a lot! Have a beautiful Christmass time :-)

Tomas

On Sun, 22 Dec 2019 at 16:36, <cro...@ualberta.ca> wrote:
>
> My non-technical answer is that the reason you need z[i] (where z[i] is 1 or 0) is that the probability of detecting the species during the survey is a conditional probability. What this means is that there are 2 possibilities: 1) the species exists at the site, in which case the probability of detection is p; or 2) the species does not exist at the site, in which case the probability of detection is 0. The model is estimating p independent of pi. This is what allows it to differentiate between probability of occupancy and probability of detection. Thus, if the species was detected at least once at the site, then z[i] will be 1 in every iteration and the model is able to estimate p independently, and then apply p to the sites where the species wasn’t detected to estimate a probability of occupancy that is independent of probability of detection.
>
>
>
> If the model is written as: y[i,j] ~ dbern(pi[i] * p[i,j]), then it cannot make these independent estimates, and occupancy estimates are biased low because they are confounded with probability of detection. This give biased parameter estimates as well.
>
>
>
> Clear as mud?

>

A good way to look at this is by the marginal probability of y[i, 1:J] (data from J visits to site i).

This is written out in the second answer of the StackExchange thread you linked.  This shows that if J = 1, the marginal probabilities are equivalent, but for J > 1, they are not.  That makes sense.  For J = 1, detection probability and occupancy probability are not identifiable (setting aside single-visit occupancy ideas that bring in covariates and rely on parametric assumptions and are not the point here).  For J > 1, the probability mass function for the vector random variable y[i, 1:J] is not the same for the two models, so the models are not equivalent.

I'm confused by seeing that the StackExchange answer concludes (correctly) that the models are not the same, but I think you are saying it concludes they are the same?  Maybe there was some asynchrony in what was written when?

-Perry
